method:
member_effects measures the open-seat penalty on the party's first-preference share; seat_swing_deviation measures seats on
the two-party-preferred count with the last margin held constant, and finds a much smaller effect. This decomposes the gap.
For every seat whose member's party was Labor or the Coalition, the change in each quantity is measured against the same
party's seats with a veteran member standing again at the same election (election x party baseline, as in member_effects):
findings: When a Labor or Coalition member retires, their party's first-preference vote falls about 2.7 points relative to the same party's seats where a veteran stands again (state 2.3, federal 3.6).
Almost none of it goes to the other major party (+0.1). It goes to the Greens, independents and minor parties (+2.6), and open seats draw more candidates (+0.65 on average).
Because much of that vote flows back on preferences, the two-party cost is smaller: about 1.1 points (state 0.8, federal 1.7).
It is not regression to the mean: retiring members' seats had about the same margins as veterans' (11.2 v 10.9 points), and holding the margin constant leaves the penalty at 1.1.

The earlier gap was a baseline difference: seat_swing_deviation measured open seats against all seats, and veterans themselves run about 0.4 ahead of that. Measured against veterans, the two analyses agree (about 1 point on the two-party count).
Longer careers leave bigger holes: retirements after three or more terms cost about 3.4 points of first preferences (1.4 two-party), after one or two terms about 1.4 (0.3).
Coalition retirements cost more on the two-party count than Labor ones (about 1.8 v 0.7), with the first-preference loss similar (3.0 v 2.5).
headline: A retiring member costs ~2.7 pts of first preferences, nearly all to minors and independents; ~1.1 pts survives to the two-party count. Not regression to the mean.
